newsitem.title: UK: UK winds of change sweep Major into opposition.
newsitem.headline: UK winds of change sweep Major into opposition.

text.p: Winds of change, reaching hurricane force, blew John Major into the political wilderness on Friday after 6-1/2 years of turmoil, personal vilification and occasional pockets of glory as prime minister.

Three times in his career Major, the most "ordinary" man to hold the top job in British politics, has benefited from his reputation as a safe choice, someone who could be trusted to do the right thing.

But his sure touch failed him during the longest election campaign in 80 years. The "grey man" of British politics was unable to dent the popularity of New Labour and its leader Tony Blair, much more a politician of the media-dominated 1990s.

Despite being the centrepiece of his Conservative Party's campaign to clinch a record fifth election victory in a row, Major was unable to defeat what he called his "phantom enemy" -- British voters' desire to change government after 18 years.
Labour swept to power in Thursday's election with a huge projected majority of 179. Blair succeeds Major as Britain's youngest prime minister this century.

In 1990, it was all so different for Major. After the bloody despatch of "Iron Lady" Margaret Thatcher, the Conservatives were looking for a calming influence in 10, Downing Street and they looked no further than her finance minister, John Major.

Two years later, the opinion polls showed the Conservatives were heading for election defeat but voters at the last minute turned away from Neil Kinnock's Labour Party for the safety of the prime minister it knew -- Major.
But Major's victory at that election, probably his finest hour, was overshadowed by his humiliating withdrawal of sterling from Europe's Exchange Rate Mechanism in September 1992.
That sparked rows over how close Britain should align itself with the European Union that dogged the rest of his premiership.
Eurosceptic right-wingers continually snapped at his heels, demanding he rule out joining a European single currency, due to start in 1999.

Major, who went into the 1997 election saying he would wait and see whether the currency was in Britain's interest, finally snapped in mid-1995, resigning the Conservative leadership and telling party rebels to "put up or shut up".

Cabinet minister John Redwood was the only malcontent to stand against Major under the banner "No change, no chance". Major swatted him aside but the Eurosceptics remained stridently opposed to his European policy.
He staggered on, hoping his party's popularity would increase. But Labour held a 20-point lead when he was finally forced to call an election, at the last possible moment.
Major, unveiling what he called the boldest and most far-reaching manifesto any party had published since 1979, tackled head on Blair's claim that a chanage was needed.

"It is time for a change. Time for a change to the next phase of Conservative prosperity that will give everyone -- no matter who they are, where they live -- more choice and more control over their lives," Major said.

But he was whistling in the wind and the voters were determined to end it for the Conservatives, a party traditionally run by the rich and privileged, and its leader, a working class boy who left school at 16.
Major, born in south London on March 29, 1943, saw poverty first-hand as a child.
His father, originally a trapeze artist in a vaudeveille act, had a factory making garden gnome ornaments that went bust, forcing the Majors to swop their family home for a small apartment.
He did several different jobs before going into banking. He worked in Hong Kong and Nigeria, where he suffered a serious leg injury in a car crash that still affects his walking.

He entered parliament in 1979 as member for Huntingdon, north of London. He was spotted by Conservative talent scouts working in local politics in the working class London suburb of Lambeth, a Labour Party stronghold.
He rose to become Minster of Social Security and in 1987 Chief Secretary (junior minister) to the Treasury.
Major was then unexpectedly catapulted into the spotlight when Thatcher made him Foreign Secretary in July 1989.
Three months later, he became Chancellor of the Exchequer (finance Minister), articulating Thatcher's anti-inflation policy and his own gradualist approach to European Monetary Union.
Once in power he fought doggedly to bring peace to Northern Ireland, one of the 20th century's most insoluble guerrilla conflicts, even though his efforts provided few political gains.
He reacted with icy calm when Irish Republican Army guerrillas mortar-bombed his Downing Street residence. His quiet authority during the Gulf War sent his popularity soaring.
But his turbulent years in power tend to be remembered more for the lows than the highs -- party mutinies, resignations sparked by scandals, embarrassing policy U-turns.

The greatest passion of this self-effacing and essentially private man is sport. He regularly attends Chelsea soccer club games and has the results of cricket internationals relayed to his plane when he is away on foreign trips.
Major's wife Norma, whom he married in 1970, is a fervent opera fan. In 1987, she published a biography of Australian soprano Joan Sutherland and did much to promote a boost in opera's popularity.
The Majors have two grown-up children, Elizabeth and James.
